passages.quote: The specific volume (ν) of a substance is the total volume (V) of that substance divided by the total mass (m) of that substance
The density ( ρ ) of a substance is the reciprocal of its specific volume (ν).
Specific gravity (S.G.) is a measure of the relative density of a substance as compared to the density of water at a standard temperature.
Humidity is the amount of moisture (water vapor) in the air.
An intensive property is independent of the amount of mass. The value of an extensive property varies directly with the mass.
Temperature is a measure of the molecular activity of a substance.
The zero points on both absolute scales represent the same physical state.
Absolute zero = -460 °F or -273 °C
What is the Rankine equivalent of 80°C?
almost all pressure gauges register zero when open to the atmosphere.
14.7 psia = 408 inches of water
Mass and total volume are examples of extensive properties.
for water at 14.7 psia, the saturation temperature is 212°F.
1 Btu = 778.3 ft-lbf
Pressure is a measure of the force exerted per unit area on the boundaries of a substance (or system).
When pressure is measured relative to a perfect vacuum, it is called absolute pressure (psia); when measured relative to atmospheric pressure (14.7 psi), it is called gauge pressure (psig).
If the pressure is below that of the atmosphere, it is designated as a vacuum.
Energy is defined as the capacity of a system to perform work or produce heat.
Potential energy (PE) is defined as the energy of position.
Kinetic energy (KE) is the energy of motion.
These microscopic forms of energy are collectively called internal energy, customarily represented by the symbol U.
This form of energy is called P-V energy because it arises from the pressure (P) and the volume (V) of a fluid.
Specific enthalpy (h) is defined as h = u + Pν
Work is a form of energy, but it is energy in transit.
A positive value for work indicates that work is done by the system on its surroundings; a negative value indicates that work is done on the system by its surroundings.
Heat, like work, is energy in transit.
A positive value for heat indicates that heat is added to the system by its surroundings.
The heat added to or removed from a substance to produce a change in its temperature is called sensible heat.
Latent heat is the amount of heat added to or removed from a substance to produce a change in phase.
When latent heat is added, no temperature change occurs.
The heat capacity of a substance per unit mass is called the specific heat (cp) of the substance.
Entropy quantifies the energy of a substance that is no longer available to perform useful work.
Power is defined as the time rate of doing work.
A system in thermodynamics is nothing more than the collection of matter that is being studied.
Everything external to the system is called the thermodynamic surroundings
An isolated system is one that is not influenced in any way by the surroundings.
A closed system has no transfer of mass with its surroundings, but may have a transfer of energy (either heat or work) with its surroundings.
An open system is one that may have a transfer of both mass and energy with its surroundings.
A control volume is a fixed region in space chosen for the thermodynamic study of mass and energy balances for flowing systems.
Steady state is that circumstance in which there is no accumulation of mass or energy within the control volume, and the properties at any point within the system are independent of time.
Therefore, at the conclusion of a cycle, all the properties have the same value they had at the beginning.
In reality, there are no truly reversible processes
Four of the most common causes of irreversibility are friction, unrestrained expansion of a fluid, heat transfer through a finite temperature difference, and mixing of two different substances.
An adiabatic process is one in which there is no heat transfer into or out of the system.
An isentropic process is one in which the entropy of the fluid remains constant.
A throttling process is defined as a process in which there is no change in enthalpy from state one to state two, h1 = h2; no work is done, W = 0; and the process is adiabatic, Q = 0.
The term saturation defines a condition in which a mixture of vapor and liquid can exist together at a given temperature and pressure.
The higher the pressure, the higher the saturation temperature.
its quality (x) is defined as the ratio of the mass of the vapor to the total mass of both vapor and liquid.
The moisture content of a substance is the opposite of its quality.
When the vapor is at a temperature greater than the saturation temperature, it is said to exist as superheated vapor.
Sublimation is a special term used for cases in which the transition between the solid phase and the vapor phase occurs directly, without passing through the liquid phase.
the triple point, defined as the state in which all three phases may be present in equilibrium.
at the critical point the saturated-liquid and saturated-vapor states are identical.
So the processes of vaporization and condensation are the exact opposite of each other.
A T-s diagram is the type of diagram most frequently used to analyze energy transfer system cycles.
the heat transferred to or from a system equals the area under the T-s curve of the process.
The Mollier diagram is used only when quality is greater than 50% and for superheated steam.
Steam tables consist of two sets of tables of the energy transfer properties of water and steam: saturated steam tables and superheated steam tables.
Usually, two properties (for example, v, p, T, h, s) of the substance must be known in order to determine the other needed properties.
Energy can neither be created nor destroyed, only altered in form.
all energies into the system are equal to all energies leaving the system plus the change in storage of energies within the system.
there is no change in storage (i.e. heat exchangers do not swell while in operation).
The control volume approach is usually used today in analyzing thermodynamic systems.
enthalpy, has been defined as h = u + Pν.
These would be classified as isothermal, isobaric, or isovolumetric processes, respectively.
It is important to note that the later equation can only be used when no phase change occurs since ∆T = 0 during a phase change.
each component of the system is thermodynamically analyzed as an open system as the fluid passes through it.
The condensation process is the heat-rejection mechanism for the cycle.

It is impossible to construct a device that operates in a cycle and produces no effect other than the removal of heat from a body at one temperature and the absorption of an equal quantity of heat by a body at a higher temperature.
It is impossible to construct an engine that will work in a complete cycle and produce no other effect except the raising of a weight and the cooling of a heat reservoir.
the second law denies the possibility of completely converting into work all of the heat supplied to a system operating in a cycle
However, no information about the direction of the process can be obtained by the application of the first law.
Entropy can also be explained as a measure of the unavailability of heat to perform work in a cycle.
entropy must increase or stay the same for a cyclic system; it can never decrease.
No engine can be more efficient than a reversible engine operating between the same high temperature and low temperature reservoirs.
The efficiency of a reversible engine depends only upon the temperatures of the heat source and heat receiver.
the Carnot efficiency serves as an unattainable upper limit for any real system’s efficiency.
These isentropic processes will be represented by vertical lines on either T-s or h-s diagrams
the dashed lines representing the real process will slant slightly towards the right since the entropy will increase from the start to the end of the process.

The efficiency of each type of component can be calculated by comparing the actual work produced by the component to the work that would have been produced by an ideal component operating isentropically between the same inlet and outlet conditions.
An actual turbine does less work because of friction losses in the blades, leakage past the blades and, to a lesser extent, mechanical friction.
A pump requires more work because of unavoidable losses due to friction and fluid turbulence.
The main feature of the Rankine cycle, shown in Figure 31, is that it confines the isentropic compression process to the liquid phase only
excessive condenser subcooling will decrease cycle efficiency.
Turbines, pumps, and compressors all behave non-ideally due to heat losses, friction and windage losses.
Another example of a loss due to a system’s design is heat loss to the environment
the pressure of a gas expanding at constant temperature varies inversely to the volume
the pressure of a gas varies directly with temperature when the volume is held constant, and the volume varies directly with temperature when the pressure is held constant
where the pressure and temperature are absolute values.
No real gases follow the ideal gas law or equation completely.
results in work performed on the system and is essentially the area under a P-V curve.
A fluid is any substance that conforms to the shape of its container.
The predominant effect of an increase in pressure in a compressible fluid, such as a gas, is an increase in the density of the fluid.
An increase in the pressure of an incompressible fluid will not have a significant effect on the density.
An increase in temperature will tend to decrease the density of any fluid.
A 5% increase in absolute temperature will result in a 5% increase in the absolute pressure.
this results in a tremendous increase in pressure for a relatively minor temperature change.
pressure in a water-solid system will increase about 100 psi for every 1 °F increase in temperature.
No engine, actual or ideal, when operating in a cycle can convert all the heat supplied it into mechanical work-heat must be rejected.

body.text: The mass of a body is the measure of the amount of material present in it. Its weight is the force exerted when that mass is accelerated in a gravitational field.
wt = mg / gc, with g = 32.17 ft/sec² and gc = 32.17 lbm-ft/lbf-sec²
The mass of a body stays constant even if the gravitational acceleration acting on it changes.
Because the density of a fluid varies with temperature, specific gravities must be specified at particular temperatures.
Absolute humidity is the mass of water vapor per unit volume of air. Relative humidity is the water vapor present divided by the maximum the air could contain at that temperature, as a percentage.
Temperature, pressure, specific volume, and density are intensive. Mass and total volume are extensive.

checks.q: How are density and specific volume related?
o: Density is the reciprocal of specific volume
Density is specific volume times mass
checks.x: The density of a substance is the reciprocal of its specific volume.

checks.q: A quantity of matter is divided into two equal parts. What happens to its intensive properties?
o: Each part keeps the same value
Each part has half the value
Each part has twice the value
checks.x: An intensive property is independent of the amount of mass, so each part has the same value as the original.

checks.q: Which of these is an extensive property?
checks.x: Mass and total volume are extensive. Temperature, pressure, and density are intensive.

body.text: The greater the movement of molecules, the higher the temperature. Temperature can be used to predict the direction of heat transfer.
The Celsius scale has 100 units between the freezing point and boiling point of water at standard atmospheric pressure, and the Fahrenheit scale has 180.
The Kelvin scale is the absolute scale that corresponds to Celsius, and the Rankine scale is the absolute scale that corresponds to Fahrenheit.

body.alt: Two pairs of scales: 212 °F is 672 °R, 32 °F is 492 °R, and -460 °F is 0 °R; 100 °C is 373 K, 0 °C is 273 K, and -273 °C is 0 K.

checks.x: The handbook gives absolute zero as -460 °F or -273 °C.

body.text: Pressure is caused by the collisions of molecules with the boundaries of the system. It is frequently measured in lbf/in² (psi).
Almost all pressure gauges register zero when open to the atmosphere, so they measure the difference between the fluid pressure and the surrounding air.

body.alt: Diagram of pressure levels: gauge pressure is measured up from atmospheric pressure, vacuum is measured down from it, and absolute pressure is measured up from a perfect vacuum.

items: 1 inch of mercury = 25.4 millimeters of mercury
1 millimeter of mercury = 10³ microns of mercury

checks.q: What does a pressure gauge open to the atmosphere normally read?
checks.x: Almost all pressure gauges register zero when open to the atmosphere.

checks.q: Using the handbook's conversions, 14.7 psia equals how many inches of water?
checks.x: 14.7 psia equals 408 inches of water and 29.9 inches of mercury.

body.text: PE = mgz / gc
KE = mv² / 2gc
The specific internal energy of a substance is its internal energy per unit mass, u = U/m.
A fluid under pressure has the capacity to perform work. P-V energy is also called flow energy.
Enthalpy is a property of a substance, but it cannot be measured directly. It is the change in specific enthalpy, not the absolute value, that is important in practical problems.
Enthalpy represents the total energy of a system, as the sum of internal energy and flow energy.
body.cite: Word: Basic Energy Concepts 6-11.docx, slide 1.18 Enthalpy

checks.q: Which equation defines specific enthalpy?
checks.x: Specific enthalpy is defined as h = u + Pν.

checks.q: What is P-V energy also called?
checks.x: P-V energy arises from the pressure and volume of a fluid and is also called flow energy.

body.text: Work is not a property of a system. A system contains no work.
W = Fd
Heat transfer occurs at the molecular level as a result of a temperature difference. In engineering, the unit of heat is the British thermal unit (Btu).
The latent heat of fusion changes phase between solid and liquid. The latent heat of vaporization changes phase between liquid and vapor, and is sometimes called the latent heat of condensation.
cp = Q / (m∆T), so Q = m cp ∆T
Heat and work are both boundary phenomena. Both represent energy crossing the system boundary, and systems never possess either one.

checks.q: What is sensible heat?
o: Heat that changes a substance's phase at constant temperature
Heat that changes a substance's temperature
checks.x: Heat added or removed to produce a change in temperature is sensible heat.

checks.q: What happens to temperature while latent heat is added?
checks.x: When latent heat is added, no temperature change occurs.

checks.q: What does a positive value for work mean in the handbook's sign convention?
o: Work is done by the system on its surroundings
Work is done on the system
Heat is added to the system
checks.x: A positive value means work is done by the system on its surroundings. A negative value means work is done on the system.

body.text: ∆S = ∆Q / Tabs    ∆s = ∆q / Tabs
Like enthalpy, entropy cannot be measured directly. It is given with respect to a reference value.

checks.q: One Btu equals about how many foot-pounds-force?
checks.x: 1 Btu = 778.3 ft-lbf. This relationship is often used to convert mechanical energy to Btu.

body.text: The system is separated from the surroundings by the system boundaries, which may be fixed or movable.
A system is in thermodynamic equilibrium when it is in equilibrium with regard to all possible changes in state. A gas in thermal equilibrium has the same temperature throughout.

checks.q: Which type of system allows both mass and energy to cross its boundary?
checks.x: An open system may transfer both mass and energy with its surroundings.

checks.q: What can cross the boundary of a closed system?
checks.x: A closed system has no transfer of mass but may transfer heat or work.

checks.q: What describes steady state?
o: No flow across the control surface
No accumulation of mass or energy in the control volume, with properties independent of time
checks.x: At steady state nothing accumulates in the control volume and the properties at any point do not change with time.

body.text: The path of the succession of states through which a system passes is called the thermodynamic process.
When a system returns to its initial values after a number of changes in state, it has undergone a cyclic process or cycle.
A reversible process can be reversed, leaving no change in the system or surroundings.
An irreversible process cannot return both the system and the surroundings to their original conditions.
An isentropic process results if the process is reversible and adiabatic.
In a polytropic process, a plot of Log P against Log V is a straight line, so PVⁿ is a constant.
An example of a throttling process is an ideal gas flowing through a valve in midposition. Pressure drops and velocity rises.

checks.q: A process is both reversible and adiabatic. What kind of process is it?
checks.x: Entropy stays constant if the process is reversible and adiabatic, so it is isentropic.

checks.q: Which is one of the most common causes of irreversibility?
checks.x: The four most common causes are friction, unrestrained expansion, heat transfer through a finite temperature difference, and mixing of different substances.

body.text: An extensive property may be made intensive by dividing it by the total mass. Any specific property is an intensive property.
The saturation temperature is the temperature at which vaporization starts for a given pressure. The saturation pressure is the pressure at which it starts for a given temperature.

body.alt: Graph of pressure against temperature with a rising vapor pressure curve.

body.text: The graph of temperature against pressure at saturated conditions is called the vapor pressure curve.
A liquid below the saturation temperature for its pressure is called subcooled or compressed liquid. Both terms have the same meaning.
M = 1 - x

items: Sublimation: change of phase from solid to vapor
Vaporization: change of phase from liquid to vapor
Condensation: change of phase from vapor to liquid
Fusion or melting: change of phase from solid to liquid

checks.q: A mixture has 0.2 lbm of vapor and 0.8 lbm of liquid at saturation. What is its moisture content?
checks.x: Moisture is the liquid mass over the total mass, 0.8, and M = 1 - x.

checks.q: What is the change of phase directly from solid to vapor called?
checks.x: Sublimation is the transition between the solid and vapor phases without passing through the liquid phase.

checks.q: What defines the triple point?
o: The pressure at which boiling begins
The state in which all three phases may be present in equilibrium
The point above which liquid and vapor are the same
checks.x: The triple point is the state in which all three phases may be in equilibrium.

body.text: For water at 212 °F the saturation pressure is 14.7 psia, and at 14.7 psia the saturation temperature is 212 °F.

body.text: On the T-V diagram, the line from A to B heats liquid to saturation, the line from B to C is the constant-temperature change from liquid to vapor, and the line from C to D superheats the steam.
At a pressure of 3206.2 psia there is no constant-temperature vaporization process. The critical temperature is 705.47 °F.

checks.q: On a T-s diagram, what does the area under the curve of a process represent?
o: The heat transferred to or from the system
checks.x: By the definition of entropy, the heat transferred equals the area under the T-s curve of the process.

checks.q: At 14.7 psia, what is the saturation temperature of water?
checks.x: For water at 14.7 psia the saturation temperature is 212 °F.

body.text: The Mollier diagram plots enthalpy against entropy. It has lines of constant temperature, pressure, moisture or quality, and superheat.
Saturated tables come as temperature tables, listed by saturation temperature, and pressure tables, listed by saturation pressure.
h = xhg + (1 - x)hf    x = (h - hf) / hfg
The same form applies to specific volume and specific entropy.

checks.q: How many properties must usually be known to determine a substance's other properties?
checks.x: Usually two properties must be known to determine the others.

body.text: The open system is the most general of the three types. Isolated and closed systems are specialized cases of it.

body.alt: Sketches of an isolated system, a control mass (closed system) with energy changes, and an open system with mass crossing the boundary.

body.text: ṁ(hin + pein + kein) + Q̇ = ṁ(hout + peout + keout) + Ẇ
Energy caused by neither mass nor shaft work is classified as heat energy.

checks.q: In open system analysis, which two terms are combined into enthalpy?
checks.x: The u and Pν terms occur so often that enthalpy was defined as h = u + Pν.

checks.q: Which approach is usually used today to analyze thermodynamic systems?
checks.x: The control volume approach is usually used because it is more convenient and requires less work to keep track of energy balances.

body.text: In a heat exchanger, the heat transfer rate can be calculated with Q̇ = ṁ(hout - hin) or Q̇ = ṁcp∆T.
The first equation can be used for a phase change heat transfer process as well as for latent heat calculations.
ṁ1(hout,1 - hin,1) = -ṁ2(hout,2 - hin,2)
Both sides of a heat exchanger have their own energy balances as the heat energy is transferred from one fluid to the other.
Processes that increase specific enthalpy include the reactor, where heat is added, and the pump. Heat exchangers, where heat is removed, decrease it. Throttle valves do not change it.

body.text: For a turbine, the decrease in the enthalpy of the working fluid equals the work done by the fluid. For a pump, the increase in enthalpy equals the work done on the fluid.

checks.q: Why can Q̇ = ṁcp∆T not be used across a phase change?
o: Because cp becomes infinite only for gases
checks.x: The equation can only be used when no phase change occurs, since ∆T = 0 during a phase change.

bc: constant pressure transfer of heat in the boiler

body.alt: Steam plant loop: steam generator to turbine, condenser, condensate pump, feed pump, and back to the steam generator.

body.text: In a typical steam plant cycle, vapor from the steam generator is expanded in the turbine, condensed in the condenser, and pumped back to the steam generator.

checks.q: In a steam plant cycle, what is the heat-rejection mechanism?
checks.x: The condensation process is the heat-rejection mechanism for the cycle.

body.text: Natural processes proceed in a certain direction, such as heat transfer from a hot to a cold body. The second law explains this.
∆S = ∆Q / Tabs (for a reversible process)
Second law problems are treated much like first law problems, with an isolated, closed, or open system chosen by the energy crossing the boundary.

checks.q: What does the second law deny?
o: Completely converting into work all of the heat supplied to a cyclic system
Any conversion of heat into work
Heat transfer from a hot to a cold body
checks.x: The second law denies the possibility of completely converting into work all of the heat supplied to a system operating in a cycle.

checks.q: What information does the second law give that the first law does not?
checks.x: The first law gives no information about the direction of the process. The second law explains it.

checks.q: For a cyclic system, how can entropy change?
o: It must increase or stay the same
checks.x: Entropy must increase or stay the same for a cyclic system. It can never decrease.

body.alt: Carnot cycle as a rectangle on a T-s diagram between TH and TC, with points 1 to 4 and a sketch of an engine between TH and TC beside it.

body.text: The Carnot cycle has adiabatic compression, isothermal expansion as heat is added at TH, adiabatic expansion, and isothermal compression as heat is removed at TC.
η = (TH - TC) / TH = 1 - (TC / TH), with temperatures in °R
Maximum possible efficiency exists when TH is at its largest possible value or TC is at its smallest value.

body.text: ηt = Wt,actual / Wt,ideal
For small turbines the efficiency is generally 60% to 80%. For large turbines it is generally about 90%.
ηp = Wp,ideal / Wp,actual
Pump efficiency does not account for losses in the motor or turbine that runs the pump. Motor efficiency is the actual pump work divided by the electrical energy input.

checks.q: How is an ideal expansion shown on a T-s or h-s diagram?
checks.x: Isentropic processes are vertical lines, since entropy is on the horizontal axis and does not change.

checks.q: How is pump efficiency defined?
o: Motor input divided by pump work
Heat added divided by work out
Actual work divided by ideal work
Ideal work divided by actual work
checks.x: Pump efficiency is the ratio of the ideal work required to the actual work required.

checks.q: Why does an actual turbine do less work than an ideal turbine?
o: Friction losses in the blades, leakage past the blades, and mechanical friction
checks.x: An actual turbine does less work because of friction losses in the blades, leakage past the blades and, to a lesser extent, mechanical friction.

body.text: The heat sink for a real cycle is fixed at about 60 °F (520 °R), because the earth is the final heat sink.
Typical thermal efficiencies for fossil plants are on the order of 40%, while nuclear plants are on the order of 31%.

body.alt: Rankine cycle on a T-s diagram, with compression confined to the liquid side of the dome.

body.text: This minimizes the work to reach operating pressure and avoids the mechanical problems of pumping a two-phase mixture.
On a T-s diagram, replacing an ideal turbine with a non-ideal one reduces cycle efficiency, because unavailable energy grows more than available energy.

2-3: moist steam is dried and superheated in the moisture separator reheater
3-4 is the LP turbine expansion. 4-5: exhaust steam condenses in the condenser

body.text: Condensers are designed to subcool the liquid by 8-10 °F so the condensate pumps can pump without cavitation, but each degree of subcooling must be put back as heat.

checks.q: What is the main feature of the Rankine cycle?
o: It confines the isentropic compression to the liquid phase only
It adds all heat at the maximum temperature
checks.x: The Rankine cycle confines isentropic compression to the liquid phase, which minimizes the work needed.

checks.q: What is the effect of excessive condenser subcooling?
o: It has no effect on efficiency
It removes the need for a feed pump
checks.x: Excessive subcooling decreases cycle efficiency, because the extra heat rejected must be made up in the steam generator.

body.text: To improve a cycle's efficiency, the temperature of the heat source would be increased and the temperature of the heat sink decreased.
These losses can be seen as an increase in the system's entropy, or energy unavailable for use by the cycle.
Friction is another real world loss, both resistance to fluid flow and mechanical friction in machines.
The efficiency of a component depends on how much friction exists in the flow, the pressure drops, the inlet and outlet temperatures, and other factors.

checks.q: Which of these contributes to component inefficiency in turbines, pumps, and compressors?
o: Heat losses, friction, and windage losses
checks.x: Turbines, pumps, and compressors behave non-ideally due to heat losses, friction, and windage losses.

body.text: Boyle's law:
(P1)(V1) = (P2)(V2) = constant
Charles concluded:
Pv = RT
The ideal gas law is used because it is simple and approximates real gas behavior.

body.alt: Pressure against volume from point 1, with separate paths for constant pressure, constant temperature, and constant volume.

checks.q: At constant temperature, how does the pressure of a gas vary with its volume?
checks.x: Boyle's law: the pressure of a gas expanding at constant temperature varies inversely to the volume.

checks.q: In the ideal gas equation, pressure and temperature must be expressed as what?
checks.x: In Pv = RT the pressure and temperature are absolute values.

body.text: A fluid may be considered incompressible if it is a liquid. Its density is then assumed to be constant.
Constant pressure: W1-2 = P(∆V)    Constant volume: W1-2 = V(∆P)
A gas in a fixed volume responds to a temperature change as the ideal gas laws predict.
An incompressible liquid in a closed container tries to expand as its temperature rises, but the walls prevent it.

checks.q: What is the effect of a temperature rise on a liquid-filled closed container?
o: A drop in density with no pressure change
checks.x: Expansion is prevented by the walls, so a relatively minor temperature change causes a tremendous increase in pressure.

checks.q: A gas confined in a fixed volume has a 5% rise in absolute temperature. What happens to its absolute pressure?
checks.x: A 5% increase in absolute temperature results in a 5% increase in the absolute pressure.

checks.q: What does a pressure increase do to an incompressible fluid's density?
o: Makes it equal the gas density
checks.x: An increase in pressure of an incompressible fluid does not have a significant effect on density.

checks.q: Which equation gives the work done in a constant pressure process?
checks.x: For a constant pressure process, W1-2 = P(∆V).

facts.a: The relative density of a substance compared to the density of water at a standard temperature.

facts.q: How do intensive and extensive properties differ?
facts.a: An intensive property is independent of the amount of mass. An extensive property varies directly with the mass.
The amount of heat added to or removed from a substance to produce a change in phase, with no temperature change.
A process with no heat transfer into or out of the system.

facts.q: How do isolated, closed, and open systems differ?
facts.a: Isolated: neither mass nor energy crosses the boundary. Closed: only energy crosses. Open: both mass and energy cross.
The energy of a substance that is no longer available to perform useful work.

facts.q: What is the Carnot efficiency equation?
facts.a: η = (TH - TC)/TH, using absolute temperatures. It is an upper limit that no real system reaches.

facts.q: How does a real expansion look on a T-s diagram compared with an ideal one?
facts.a: The ideal process is a vertical line. The real process slants slightly to the right because entropy increases.

facts.q: What is the thumb rule for pressure in a water-solid system?
facts.a: Pressure rises about 100 psi for every 1 °F increase in temperature.

summary.text: Temperature is a measure of the molecular activity of a substance, and pressure is the force per unit area on its boundaries.
Heat and work are energy in transit. Sensible heat changes temperature, and latent heat changes phase.
Isolated, closed, and open systems differ in whether mass and energy cross the boundary.
The First Law says energy can neither be created nor destroyed. The energy entering a component equals the energy leaving it at steady state.
The Second Law sets the maximum efficiency of a system at the Carnot efficiency, η = (TH - TC)/TH.
Efficiency is decreased by friction, heat losses, and cycle inefficiencies.
The ideal gas law relates pressure, temperature, and volume during compression processes.
